Our Wild Democracy · Chapter 3

The Declaration
and Address

Washington, Pennsylvania · 1809
Title up. → “Last week we ended on one sentence: the church of Christ upon earth is essentially, intentionally, and constitutionally one. Today: why anyone would need to write it.” Then the Design of Religion. The hour: Design 4 · Evils and proposition 10 6 · Christendom 10 · Preamble 3 · conscience and the brother 10 (break here if short: “Next week · The answer”) · the solution 3 · Propositions 10 · our table 8 · reception and proof-sheets 5.
The Address

The Design of Religion

Start here. The Address is the long part, to “all that love our Lord Jesus Christ, in sincerity, throughout all the Churches.” Its first paragraph is the premise under everything that follows.
The Design of Religion

“That it is the grand design and native tendency of our holy religion to reconcile and unite men to God, and to each other, in truth and love, to the glory of God, and their own present and eternal good…”

Declaration and Address, 1809
• Stop before “will not, we presume, be denied.” Stand one, asked lightly: is unity what Christianity is for? If yes, every century of division is the religion failing its own purpose.
• “In truth and love”: both sides, from the first sentence. The motto later is “Union in Truth.”
The Design of Religion

“…the first and foundation truth of our Christianity is union with him, and the very next to it in order, union with each other in him.”

Declaration and Address, 1809
• The design sentence in its own order: union with him first, union with each other in him next. Unity is not a project beside the faith; it follows from it. That is proposition 1 in a sentence: given, not constructed.
• Later in the Address, the “bewildered Church has, for hundreds of years past, been rending and dividing herself into factions, for Christ’s sake, and for the truth’s sake.” The egg, in his words.
The Design of Religion

“The nativity of its Divine author was announced from heaven, by a host of angels, with high acclamations of ‘Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace and good-will toward men.’”

Declaration and Address, 1809
• Back to the first paragraph. The proof he offers is Luke 2: the religion was announced as peace.
The Design of Religion

“In so far, then, as this holy unity and unanimity in faith and love is attained, just in the same degree is the glory of God and the happiness of men promoted and secured.”

Declaration and Address, 1809
• “Just in the same degree.” Unity is not a bonus on top of the religion; it is the measure of it. Then: what does division cost?
The Address

The Evils of Division

What division costs. Practical, not doctrinal. Build the list one line at a time and let the room map each one onto now.
Proposition 10

“Division among the Christians is a horrid evil, fraught with many evils.”

“It is antichristian, as it destroys the visible unity of the body of Christ; as if he were divided against himself…”
“It is antiscriptural, as being strictly prohibited by his sovereign authority…”
“It is antinatural, as it excites Christians to contemn, to hate, and oppose one another, who are bound… to love each other as brethren…”
Declaration and Address, 1809
Three clicks, verbatim. First what division is; the Evils list that follows is what it costs. Against Christ, against Scripture, against nature: a body excommunicating part of itself. Elided from the first: “excluding and excommunicating a part of himself.” From the second: “a direct violation of his express command.” Last clause: “In a word, it is productive of confusion and of every evil work.”
→ Then what it costs.
“What awful and distressing effects have those sad divisions produced!”
“congregations broken to pieces”
“large settlements and tracts of country… entirely destitute of a Gospel ministry”
“How seldom do many… enjoy the dispensations of the Lord’s Supper, that great ordinance of unity and love”
“the tone of discipline relaxed… lest their people should leave them, and… find refuge in the bosom of another party”
“the weak stumbled, the graceless and profane hardened, the mouths of infidels opened to blaspheme religion”
Declaration and Address, 1809

(Dropped: those “who live at the door of a preached Gospel, dare not in conscience go to hear it.” Restore if useful.)
The Evils of Division

“Say, dear brethren, are not these things so?”

Declaration and Address, 1809
• His own question, to the room. Let them answer.
• → Then: it was not for want of trying. Here is fifteen hundred years of trying.

Christendom’s Search for Unity

Card. Lands after the Preamble’s despair (“amid the diversity and rancor of party contentions”) and before “anywhere but in Christ.” One click per slide. Eight to ten minutes with every slide; 1690 and 1799 are marked cuttable in their notes.

325 · Council of Nicaea

Arians against non-Arians. A creed, and fifty-six more years of war.
Constantine had just reunited the empire (324) and found the church at war over whether the Son is God. He convened the council himself. The creed condemned Arius with the word homoousios.
Failure: Constantine was baptized on his deathbed by an Arian sympathizer; his son pushed the empire Arian; Athanasius was exiled five times. Jerome: “the whole world groaned and found itself Arian.”
→ The first creed written to unite the church did not unite the two sides; it named them.

381 · Council of Constantinople

Is the Spirit God too? The creed we still say, the Arians outlawed, and the Goths still Arian.
Theodosius made the Nicene faith imperial law (Cunctos populos, 380) and called the council (381). It finished the creed churches say today. Thirty-six Macedonian bishops, who denied the Spirit’s full divinity, walked out.
Failure: Arianism did not die; it left the empire. The Goths, Vandals and Lombards who took the West stayed Arian into the 500s and 600s. Canon 3 ranked Constantinople second after Rome, “because it is New Rome”: the seed of 1054.
→ The council finished the creed; the emperor made it law; the church that refused it moved across the border.

431 · Council of Ephesus

Does Mary bear God? A canon forbidding new creeds, and the Church of the East gone.
Nestorius objected to Theotokos; Cyril of Alexandria opened the council before John of Antioch arrived. Each side deposed the other’s leader, and the emperor arrested both. A Formula of Reunion patched it in 433.
Canon 7 forbade any “different faith” beside Nicaea’s: the ban the next council breaks, and the one the East cites against the West in 1054.
The Church of the East (Persia) refused Ephesus and has been separate since: today the Assyrian Church of the East.
→ Plant the canon. “We will come back to that.”

451 · Council of Chalcedon

One nature or two? A Definition, “not a new creed,” and Egypt gone.
Chalcedon reaffirmed Ephesus’s ban on new creeds, then issued the Definition (“in two natures”) and said it was a definition, not a creed. The 381 creed is first read into the record here. Egypt, Armenia, Ethiopia, the Syriac churches refused it: the Oriental Orthodox, non-Chalcedonian to this day (Copts, Armenians, Ethiopians, Eritreans, Syriacs, Malankara).
→ The rhyme to plant: “not a new creed.” The thirteen propositions will say the same words.',

482 · Instrument of Union

Zeno needs Egypt back. The Henotikon, and thirty-five years of schism with Rome.
Zeno’s Henotikon (“instrument of union”), drafted with Patriarch Acacius, tried to reconcile both sides by affirming Nicaea, Ephesus and Cyril and passing over Chalcedon in silence. It did not win Egypt back. Pope Felix III excommunicated Acacius (484), and Rome and Constantinople were out of communion until 519.
→ A document literally named “instrument of union” produced the first schism between Rome and Constantinople.

1054 · The Filioque

One word added to the creed. Legates sent to settle it, and East and West apart.
The Filioque (“and the Son”) entered the creed in Spain (Toledo 589), spread through the Frankish church, and was adopted at Rome about 1014. The East objected to the content and to the unilateral change, citing Ephesus Canon 7. Cardinal Humbert’s legation (1054) also contested leavened bread and papal primacy; on 16 July he laid the bull on the altar; Patriarch Cerularius anathematized the legates. The date is conventional; the estrangement was long and the 1204 sack sealed it. Mutual anathemas lifted 1965, communion not restored.
→ How do two churches with the same creed divide over the creed? Which version, and who decides.',

1521 · The Diet of Worms

Luther before the emperor. An edict to silence him, and the West in two.
1517 the theses. Rome answers with the bull Exsurge Domine (1520) and excommunicates Luther (3 January 1521). Charles V summons him to the imperial diet at Worms; he appears on 17–18 April 1521 and will not recant. The Edict of Worms (May 1521) declares him an outlaw and bans his writings. The instrument is the emperor’s edict, meant to hold the West together; it holds nothing, and the West is in two.
We come back to this room after the Preamble: Luther at Worms is the conscience thread.
→ An edict can outlaw a man. It cannot make him recant.

1527 · Zurich

No creed this time. The magistrate. A council ruling, the sword, and Felix Manz drowned.
The one instrument on the egg that was not a creed: unity by force. After the 1525 disputations, Zurich’s council ordered infants baptized and rebaptizers banished, then (March 1526) drowned. Felix Manz died 5 January 1527, the first Protestant executed by Protestants. Schleitheim (February 1527) set out believer’s baptism and separation from the sword; Sattler was burned that May.
Six years after Worms: the first split inside Protestantism. It comes back after Proposition 9.
→ Unity by creed fails; unity by force fails worse.

1529 · The Marburg Colloquy

The Lord’s Supper. Fourteen articles agreed, and “you have a different spirit.”
Marburg Colloquy, 1–4 October 1529, called by Philip of Hesse to unite the Protestants politically and theologically. The Marburg Articles: agreement on fourteen, and on the fifteenth (the Supper) agreement on everything except whether Christ’s body is bodily present. Luther’s line to the Swiss: “Ihr habt einen andern Geist.” Lutheran and Reformed have been separate confessional families since. The Formula of Concord (1577) settled Lutheran infighting by excluding the Reformed.
→ Thomas Campbell will call the Supper “that great ordinance of unity and love.” It is the one thing they could not agree on.',

1646 · The Westminster Confession

Three kingdoms at war. One confession for all three, and two thousand ministers ejected.
Solemn League and Covenant (1643): Scotland’s price for joining Parliament’s war was a common Presbyterian settlement for all three kingdoms. The Westminster Assembly (1643–49) produced the Confession (1646) and catechisms. The Independents (the “Dissenting Brethren”) argued against Presbyterian government inside the Assembly. Parliament never fully established it in England; the Restoration (1660) restored bishops; the Act of Uniformity (1662) ejected about two thousand ministers, the Great Ejection. Scotland adopted the Confession in 1647 and keeps it. The war came first; the Confession was written during it.
The pieces: the Church of England (bishops restored), the Independents, the English Presbyterians (ejected, 1662), the Church of Scotland. The Continental Reformed were never under Westminster and are not on this slide.
→ The confession Thomas Campbell was tried under was written to unite three kingdoms. It produced nonconformity.',

1690 · The Revolution Settlement

Scotland after the Revolution. Presbytery restored, and the Covenanters outside.
William and Mary’s settlement (1690) abolished bishops and established Presbyterianism with the Westminster Confession, but without the Covenants, which the state did not renew. The Cameronians (Society People) refused to enter and became the Reformed Presbyterian Church (1743 as a presbytery). The Episcopalians went out the other side.
Cuttable: the Secession slide carries the Scottish story on its own.',

1733 · The Secession

Patrons appoint ministers. Erskine rebuked, and four ministers walk out.
The Patronage Act (1712) restored lay patrons’ right to present ministers. Erskine’s synod sermon (October 1732) attacked it; the Assembly rebuked him (1733); he and three others (Wilson, Moncrieff, Fisher) protested, were suspended, and formed the Associate Presbytery (December 1733). Deposed 1740. The Seceders renewed the Covenants; the Week 2 litany note has this.
→ His tradition began as a protest against imposed authority.',

1747 · The Burgess Oath

May a Seceder swear it? A synod vote, and mutual excommunication.
The oath, required of burgesses in Edinburgh, Glasgow and Perth: “the true religion presently professed within this realm and authorized by the laws thereof.” Burghers: it means only “not Catholic.” Anti-Burghers: it blesses the church we left. The synod split April 1747 (Associate Synod vs General Associate Synod); the Anti-Burghers excommunicated the Burghers (1748–49), and the two could not take communion together. Thomas Campbell was Anti-Burgher. The Week 2 litany note covers why it felt so large (the Testimony, the Covenants).
→ This is the rule Conemaugh broke, and the room already knows it.',

1799 · 1806 · Old Light, New Light

May the magistrate enforce religion? Revised Testimonies, and each synod in two.
The Burghers split 1799 (Original Burghers, Old Light), the Anti-Burghers 1806 (Constitutional Associate Presbytery, Old Light) over whether the civil magistrate has power in religion (Westminster Confession ch. 23). Campbell sided with the Old Lights by friendship more than conviction (Foster; Week 2 note). He sailed April 1807.
Cuttable: the Week 2 litany already told this. Keep if the room needs the landing.',

…and today

Too many divisions to count.
The egg, shattered. Dozens of pieces, many of them named, the names chosen to make the room smile (four kinds of Church of Christ are in there). No click; it is simply on screen.
→ Every one of these was somebody’s instrument of unity.
The tree of divisions
Every branch is a church leaving another, placed at its year; time runs left to right, with the Reformation given most of the width. The leaves at the right edge are churches that still exist. Simplified and partial on purpose: the real tree does not fit on a wall.
→ Not one of these produced unity. Not one held even the people who signed it.
The Declaration

Preamble

The sentiments of the people of the grove.
Summer 1809. The people following Thomas Campbell from farmhouse to maple grove have become something, and they need to say what. The Declaration is the short part, written for them. After the egg: this is what the people of the grove wanted, and why they despaired of getting it the old way.
Preamble

“…tired and sick of the bitter jarrings and janglings of a party spirit, we would desire to be at rest; and, were it possible, we would also desire to adopt and recommend such measures as would give rest to our brethren throughout all the churches…”

Declaration and Address, 1809
• The line everyone remembers. Say it slowly. “Rest” is the word they chose, not “victory.”
Preamble

“This desirable rest, however, we utterly despair either to find for ourselves, or to be able to recommend to our brethren, by continuing amid the diversity and rancor of party contentions, the veering uncertainty and clashings of human opinions…”

Declaration and Address, 1809
• Stop here. Do not read the next clause yet.
• → Before the answer, name the issue underneath all of it. Why can none of those instruments work?

Why did every instrument fail?

Card. Fifteen hundred years of creeds, councils and swords, and a document that despairs of the old way. The next slide names the reason underneath.
Anton von Werner, Luther at the Diet of Worms, 1877 · public domain
Worms, 1521

Conscience cannot
be compelled.

Asked to recant. (“Here I stand, I can do no other” is the famous form; the earliest printed accounts add it, the transcript does not. Say “as the story goes.”)
→ This is why no instrument on the egg could work: a creed can name who agrees, and a sword can make people say it, but neither can make anyone believe.
Here I stand

“…my conscience is captive to the Word of God. I cannot and will not recant anything, since it is neither safe nor right to go against conscience.”

Martin Luther at Worms, 18 April 1521
• The line everyone remembers. Say it slowly. (“Here I stand, I can do no other” is the famous form; the earliest printed accounts add it, the transcript does not.)
• → Then what conscience is, and the whole sentence it ends.

Conscience is not “I can do what I want.”

It is “I must.”
One click. His word is captive: bound, not free. Conscience here is not a preference but an obligation before God. “Neither safe nor right to go against conscience”: not safe, because he must answer to God for it.
Worms, 18 April 1521

“Unless I am convinced by the testimony of the Scriptures or by clear reason… I am bound by the Scriptures… and my conscience is captive to the Word of God. I cannot and will not recant anything, since it is neither safe nor right to go against conscience. May God help me. Amen.”

Martin Luther at Worms, 18 April 1521
• The whole sentence, two trims on screen: “I have quoted,” and the parenthesis “(for I do not trust either in the pope or in councils alone, since it is well known that they have often erred and contradicted themselves).” Councils have erred: the egg, in his words.
• Note how it starts: “Unless I am convinced.” He holds his own reading open to correction. That is the opposite of “I can do what I want.” (Translations vary; this is the common English form.)

Word of God≠interpretations of the Word of God

Two clicks. What Luther is captive to. Not the pope’s reading, not a council’s, not even his own: “Unless I am convinced by the testimony of the Scriptures or by clear reason.” He can be corrected by the Word, so his reading is not the Word. That is what keeps conscience from becoming “I can do what I want”: it answers to something outside itself.
Luther did not invent this

Even a mistaken
conscience binds.

Thomas Aquinas, c. 1270 · paraphrased
Aquinas, two and a half centuries before Worms, Summa Theologiae I-II q.19 a.5 (“whether an erring conscience binds”): “every will at variance with reason, whether right or erring, is always evil.” Even believing in Christ, willed against one’s reason, is evil.
→ Rome condemned Luther; it never stopped teaching this.
(Avoid the Aquinas line about dying excommunicated, Sentences IV d.38: its meaning is disputed.)
“A human being must always obey the certain judgment of his conscience.”Catechism of the Catholic Church, 1992
“He must not be forced to act contrary to his conscience.”Vatican II, 1965
Two clicks. The same teaching, in Rome’s own words today.
• Catechism §1790 continues: “If he were deliberately to act against it, he would condemn himself.”
• Vatican II, Dignitatis Humanae §3 (Catechism §1782): “No merely human power can either command or prohibit acts of this kind.”
• The honest gap: Gregory XVI, Mirari Vos (1832), called liberty of conscience for everyone “that absurd and erroneous proposition.” Rome reached Campbell’s conclusion in 1965.
→ Back to the egg: you can compel conformity; you cannot compel communion.
Why it binds

“His conscience is man’s most secret core and his sanctuary. There he is alone with God, whose voice echoes in his depths.”

Catechism of the Catholic Church §1776 · quoting Vatican II
• Why it binds: conscience is where a person stands before God with no one in between, and that is what a priest is. Catechism §1546: “The whole community of believers is, as such, priestly.”
• Source: Gaudium et Spes §16, which opens: “a law which he has not laid upon himself but which he must obey.” That is “I must.”
The Catechism

“Conscience is the aboriginal Vicar of Christ.”

John Henry Newman, 1875 · quoted in the Catechism of the Catholic Church §1778
• Let it sit. “Aboriginal” means first: before pope or council, Christ’s first representative in a person is conscience. And it is in the Catechism.
• Newman, Letter to the Duke of Norfolk (1875) §5. Same letter: “I shall drink—to the Pope, if you please,—still, to Conscience first, and to the Pope afterwards.”
Luther, a year before Worms

“…whoever comes out of the water of baptism can boast that he is already a consecrated priest, bishop, and pope…”

No one can stand before God in your place.
So no one can read the Word in your place.
Martin Luther, To the Christian Nobility of the German Nation, 1520 · Luther’s Works 44
• One click. A year before Worms: “we are all consecrated priests through baptism, as St. Peter says in I Peter 2[:9].” No one can stand before God for you.
• The sentence goes on: “although of course it is not seemly that just anybody should exercise such office.”

Priesthood of all believers

Every believer: the Spirit within, united with Christ, answering to God directly.
Card, one click. The ground under Worms: why conscience is an obligation and not a preference. No one can stand before God in your place, so no one can read the Word in your place either. It names what the last slides have shown, Catholic and Luther alike. Then Worms beside Washington, and Marburg: Luther could not grant it to Zwingli.

How far can
Luther take this?

He has claimed conscience for himself, before the emperor. Ask it plainly: will he grant it to the next man? Then Marburg.
August Noack, Religionsgespräch zu Marburg 1529 (detail), 1867–69 · public domain
Marburg · October 1529

Luther and Zwingli.

He could not share the Lord’s table with a brother who read the Lord’s table differently.
The painting (detail): Luther, in the fur collar, holds Zwingli off; Zwingli points upward. In the full canvas Luther’s hand is on est chalked on the table (“this is my body”). Fourteen articles agreed; on the fifteenth, everything but the bodily presence. Luther: “Ihr habt einen andern Geist”, “You have a different spirit.” As the accounts have it, he would not take Zwingli’s hand as a brother’s.
→ Two men, both captive to the same Word. Only one would grant the other that.
Black.

Luther claimed conscience for himself.
Campbell claimed it for his brother.

Say it once and stop. Not a new principle: the same principle, extended to the brother. Luther is not the villain here: the man of Worms and the man of Marburg were equally sincere. That is the point: conscience claimed for yourself is only half a sentence, and Campbell finishes it. This is the chapter in one line.
Preamble

“…as no man can be judged for his brother, so no man can judge for his brother; every man must be allowed to judge for himself, as every man must bear his own judgment—must give account of himself to God.”

Declaration and Address, 1809
• The Preamble’s second sentence: the half Luther could not say at Marburg. Not a right claimed but an impossibility stated: you cannot believe for someone else. Zurich and 1806 on the egg were the magistrate trying. The first sentence, just before it: “it is high time for us not only to think, but also to act, for ourselves… to this alone we feel ourselves Divinely bound to be conformed, as by this alone, we must be judged.”
Preamble

“That every such judgment is an express violation of the law of Christ, a daring usurpation of his throne, and a gross intrusion upon the rights and liberties of his subjects.”

Declaration and Address, 1809
• The very next sentence. “Such judgment” is the one just before it: “no man has a right to judge his brother, except in so far as he manifestly violates the express letter of the law.” Whoever judges his brother’s conscience is sitting on Christ’s throne.
The Appendix

“…judging and rejecting each other in matters wherein the Lord hath not judged, in a flat contradiction to his expressly revealed will.”

Declaration and Address, 1809
• The Appendix names this as one of two great evils provoking the Lord against the churches; the other is “the taking and giving of unjust offenses.” He then quotes James 4:12: “There is one Lawgiver, who is able to save and to destroy: who art thou that judgest another?” And: “we judge him, not for his opinions, but for his presumption.”

Proposition 9

“…members of the same body, subjects of the same grace, objects of the same Divine love, bought with the same price, and joint-heirs of the same inheritance. Whom God hath thus joined together no man should dare to put asunder.”

Declaration and Address, 1809
• The marriage line, turned on the brother. Every phrase is something God did, not something we agreed to. If God joined them, rejecting a brother is putting asunder what God joined.
• Proposition 9 returns in full in the Propositions section.
Worms · 1521

Rome rejects Luther.

Four slides, no clicks, one beat each. Same rhythm every time; let the room hear the pattern before you name it. Rome: excommunication (January 1521), then the Edict of Worms (May 1521) makes him an outlaw.
Marburg · 1529

Luther rejects Zwingli.

The man rejected at Worms, eight years later: “You have a different spirit.” No common table over the bodily presence.
Zurich · 1527

Zwingli rejects the Anabaptists.

His own students, Grebel and Manz, over infant baptism. Zurich’s council, with Zwingli’s support, made rebaptism a capital crime (March 1526); Felix Manz was drowned in the Limmat, 5 January 1527, the first Protestant executed by Protestants. The picture is from the Martyrs Mirror, the Anabaptists’ own book of martyrs: an Anabaptist held under at the riverbank, as Manz was in the Limmat. (Zurich’s own chronicle shows Manz’s drowning too: Heinrich Thomann’s 1605 copy of Bullinger.) Two years later, at Marburg, Zwingli would ask Luther for the hand he had refused Manz.
Each one was rejected for his conscience, and each one rejected the next man for his.
Washington, Pennsylvania · 1809

How dare you put asunder?

Then Campbell, turning Proposition 9 on all of them: “Whom God hath thus joined together no man should dare to put asunder.” Not one of the four was rejected for denying Christ. Each was rejected by a brother. Pause before moving on.

◆ for discussion

What is beautiful here? What do we carry forward?

Backup prompts (off the slide): Who have we treated the way Luther treated Zwingli, over a reading of Scripture? What instrument do we reach for when we want unity: a statement, a rule, a vote?
If the room is slow: “Have you ever been the brother someone else judged for?”
Idea 1 of 7

Unity is the design of religion.

“The grand design and native tendency of our holy religion” is to unite us to God and to each other. Union with him first; union with each other in him next. From the Design of Religion: “the first and foundation truth of our Christianity is union with him, and the very next to it in order, union with each other in him.”
Idea 2 of 7

Division is a horrid evil.

Not a difference of opinion: a wound in the body of Christ. Proposition 10: “antichristian, as it destroys the visible unity of the body of Christ.” And the Evils of Division litany.
Idea 3 of 7

Every instrument failed.

Creeds, councils, edicts, swords: each was offered for unity, and each left another division. The egg, 325 to 1806.
Idea 4 of 7

Conscience cannot be compelled.

It binds because there you answer to God, as his priest. Worms; Aquinas; Vatican II and the Catechism (“alone with God”); Newman; Luther in 1520 on the baptized as priests.
Idea 5 of 7

Conscience is an exercise of the priesthood of all believers.

Why conscience binds: it is where each believer stands before God, as his priest. The Catechism (“alone with God”; “the whole community of believers is, as such, priestly”); Newman (“the aboriginal Vicar of Christ”); Luther in 1520 (“a consecrated priest, bishop, and pope”).
Idea 6 of 7

Commitment to the Word of God, not interpretations of the Word of God.

Luther at Worms: “Unless I am convinced by the testimony of the Scriptures or by clear reason.” Captive to the Word itself: not the pope’s reading, not a council’s, not even his own. That is what keeps conscience from becoming “I can do what I want.”
Idea 7 of 7

No one may judge for his brother.

Luther claimed conscience for himself; Campbell claimed it for his brother. The Preamble (“no man can judge for his brother”), the Appendix (“We dare not… patronize the rejection of God’s dear children”), Proposition 9, and the chain of rejections.
Ideas
1.Unity is the design of religion.
2.Division is a horrid evil.
3.Every instrument failed.
4.Conscience cannot be compelled.
5.Conscience is an exercise of the priesthood of all believers.
6.Commitment to the Word of God, not interpretations of the Word of God.
7.No one may judge for his brother.
All seven at once, for the room to see together before the discussion.
◆ for discussion

What is beautiful here? What do we carry forward?

Backup prompts (off the slide): Who have we treated the way Luther treated Zwingli, over a reading of Scripture? What instrument do we reach for when we want unity: a statement, a rule, a vote?
If the room is slow: “Have you ever been the brother someone else judged for?”
